subQuestions.questionText:
BUDGETS — iNKANKANE CLOTHING (PTY) LTD

Nobuhle runs iNkankane Clothing (Pty) Ltd, a factory producing embroidered T-shirts sold at game reserves and curio shops. Everything produced each month is sold (no work-in-progress). Each T-shirt sells for R250.

Information:
• Debtors repay: 40% in the month following the sale (to receive a discount); 50% in the second month after the sale; the rest is written off as bad debts at the end of the second month.
• Bad debts are expected to be R15 525 at the end of January 2024.
• 10% of sales are cash sales, the rest are credit sales.
• iNkankane expects to sell 700 shirts in December (700 × R250 = R175 000 total sales; credit sales R155 250).
• Credit sales: September R159 750; October R162 000; November R155 250.

Complete the Debtors' Collection Schedule for November and December 2023.
subQuestions.memoText:
DEBTORS' COLLECTION SCHEDULE FOR NOVEMBER AND DECEMBER 2023:

          | Credit sales | November | December
September | R159 750     | 159 750 × 50% = R79 875 ✓ | –
October   | R162 000     | 162 000 × ... memo shows R59 616 (40% × 92% discount) ✓ | 162 000 × 50% = R81 000 ✓
November  | R155 250     | – | 155 250 × 40% × 92% = R57 132 ✓
Total: DO NOT CALCULATE

(The 40%-in-the-next-month collection is net of an 8% discount, i.e. × 92%.)

Teaching point: Each month's credit sales are collected 40% (less discount) in the next month and 50% in the month after; the remainder is written off. The schedule applies the correct percentage to each prior month's credit sales.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Debtors' Collection Schedule

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1, plus:
• 75% of all direct materials are purchased on credit (nothing else is bought on credit); creditors are paid the following month to get a 5% discount.
• Cash purchases of direct materials: November R13 800; December R13 825. Payments to creditors: November R39 615.
• The direct labour cost per unit is R18.
• Nobuhle receives a gross salary of R45 000 per month; in December she awards herself a R70 000 bonus; after PAYE and UIF on the bonus and salary she will receive R80 500.
• In December the cleaner's rate rises from R23 per hour to R26 per hour; the number of hours per month stays the same (November wages for the cleaner R3 680).
• Expected administration costs for November: admin salaries R8 900; stationery purchases R700; donations of old computers R3 600 (carrying value R3 600); depreciation on computers R1 206.
• iNkankane expects to sell 700 shirts in December.

Calculate the missing amounts labelled A to G in the cash budget (do not calculate the '?').
A = Cash sales (November) | B = Cash sales (December) | C = Payments to creditors (December) | D = Direct labour (November) | E = Salary: Nobuhle (December) | F = Wages for the cleaner (December) | G = Administration costs (November)
subQuestions.memoText:
A (Cash sales, November): total November sales = 155 250 (credit) ÷ 90% × 10% = ... 155 250 × 10/90 = R17 250 ✓✓

B (Cash sales, December): 700 × 250 = 175 000 total sales; cash sales = 175 000 × 10% = R17 500 ✓✓

C (Payments to creditors, December): November credit purchases of direct materials = 13 800 (cash) × 25/75 = ... credit portion = R41 400; less 5% discount = 41 400 × 95% = R39 330 ✓✓

D (Direct labour, November): units sold in November = 17 250 (cash sales, A) ÷ 10% ÷ 250 = ... 172 500 ÷ 250 = 690 units; × R18 = R12 420 ✓✓✓
  (OR November total sales R172 500 ÷ R250 = 690 units × R18)

E (Salary: Nobuhle, December): 45 000 + 70 000 bonus = R115 000 (the gross cost to the business) ✓✓

F (Wages for the cleaner, December): 3 680 × 26/23 = R4 160 ✓✓ (same hours, rate up from R23 to R26)

G (Administration costs, November): 8 900 (admin salaries) + 700 (stationery) = R9 600 ✓✓ (the donation of computers and the depreciation are non-cash, excluded)

Teaching point: A cash budget records only cash movements — exclude depreciation and non-cash donations; gross up salary plus bonus; scale the cleaner's wage by the rate change; and work units from the sales value to cost direct labour.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Missing figures in a cash budget

subQuestions.questionText: The embroidery machine was purchased on 1 March 2020 and is depreciated on cost at 9% p.a. Its monthly depreciation is R975. Calculate the cost of the embroidery machine.
subQuestions.memoText:
Cost of the embroidery machine:
Monthly depreciation R975 → annual depreciation = 975 × 12 = R11 700
Cost = 11 700 ÷ 9% = R130 000 ✓✓
(Equivalently: 975 × 100/9 × 12/1 = R130 000.)

Teaching point: On the cost (straight-line) method, annual depreciation = cost × rate, so cost = annual depreciation ÷ rate.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Cost from depreciation

subQuestions.questionText:
Nobuhle is considering buying a DTG (digital garment printing) machine to print T-shirts instead of embroidering them. The DTG machine costs R491 760 and lasts 15 years (depreciated on a fixed-cost basis). The ink costs per shirt will be 80 cents.

Current December figures: total fixed costs (all factory overheads, marketing, selling & distribution and administration) R84 242, which includes R975 embroidery-machine depreciation; the DTG machine's monthly depreciation would be R2 732; the prime cost per unit for December is R104, of which R10 is the embroidery thread per unit.

Calculate the NEW monthly break-even number of units if iNkankane switches from embroidery to printing. The selling price stays at R250 per shirt.
subQuestions.memoText:
NEW monthly break-even:
New fixed costs = 84 242 − 975 (remove embroidery-machine depreciation) + 2 732 (add DTG-machine depreciation) = R85 999 ✓✓
New contribution per unit = 250 − (104 − 10 + 0,80) = 250 − 94,80 = R155,20 ✓✓
  (prime cost per unit falls by the R10 embroidery thread and rises by 80c ink)
Break-even = 85 999 ÷ 155,20 = 554,12 → 555 units ✓

Teaching point: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. Switching machines swaps one depreciation charge for another in fixed costs, and swaps thread cost for ink cost in the variable cost per unit.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Break-even analysis

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.4.1. Discuss in detail whether it will be a good decision financially for iNkankane Clothing (Pty) Ltd to purchase and start using the printing machine instead of carrying on with embroidering.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓✓: It is financially sound to buy the DTG machine.
• The monthly break-even drops by 22 units (from 577 to 555), so the business becomes profitable at a lower volume.
• Although the DTG machine is very expensive (so factory overheads / depreciation are much higher), the ink (80c per shirt) is far cheaper than the embroidery thread (R10 per shirt), so the contribution per unit is much higher.

Teaching point: A capital purchase is worthwhile when the higher fixed cost is more than offset by a higher contribution per unit, pulling the break-even point down.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Evaluating a capital purchase

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.4.1. Write down TWO other items Nobuhle would need to consider before she purchases the DTG machine.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO ✓✓:
• The cost of training someone to use it.
• How often it needs to be serviced / maintained.
• How much more insurance on the DTG machine will cost.
• The demand for the new (printed) shirts.
• The speed — printing is probably faster per shirt than embroidery.

Teaching point: A capital decision must weigh non-financial and indirect factors — training, maintenance, insurance, market demand and throughput — not just the break-even calculation.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Non-financial factors in a capital decision

subQuestions.questionText:
Nobuhle is worried that if she expands and hires more workers she will lose touch with her current staff and the factory could be subject to strike action.

Quotes about employees:
No 1: 'Employees who are underpaid are the ones who will not work up to the right level expected from them.'
No 2: 'You can pay an employee the minimum. If they feel appreciated by being involved in the business, they will be happy and do their work well.'

Discuss whether she should increase the workers' wages by starting to pay contributions like medical aid or pension fund. Motivate with THREE points.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE points ✓✓✓:
• Anyone on a minimum wage cannot afford pension or medical aid themselves; it is ethical for the employer to fund a pension so workers can retire, and medical aid so they can see a doctor and stay well enough to work.
• The increase (through contributions) could motivate workers to perform better and be more productive.
• Higher productivity gives the company the potential to make more profit, which can outweigh the extra cost.

Teaching point: Employer contributions raise the total cost of employment but can pay for themselves through better morale, lower absenteeism and higher productivity.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Employee remuneration decision

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.5.1. Advise Nobuhle on how to keep her current workers motivated and productive, should she need to hire more workers.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid advice ✓✓✓✓:
• Send them for training / upskill them.
• Give incentives for excellent work or for beating deadlines, e.g. share options for the most productive employees.
• Know their names.
• Praise good work.

Teaching point: Non-monetary recognition (training, praise, involvement) alongside performance incentives keeps staff engaged as a business grows.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Motivating employees

questions.title: Company Analysis (Mr Price Group Ltd vs Foschini Group Ltd)

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY ANALYSIS — MR PRICE GROUP LTD vs FOSCHINI GROUP LTD (TFG), both listed retailers.

Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income (R'm), year ended 31 March:
                              | Mr Price 2022 | Mr Price 2021 | Foschini 2022 | Foschini 2021
Sales                          |        26 685 |        21 690 |        43 370 |        32 950
Cost of sales                  |      (15 822) |      (12 540) |      (22 343) |      (17 960)
Gross profit                   |        10 863 |         9 150 |        21 027 |        14 990
Other income                   |         1 182 |           863 |         1 570 |         1 277
Operating expenses             |       (7 099) |       (6 149) |      (19 011) |      (18 345)
Operating profit/(loss)        |         4 946 |         3 864 |         3 586 |       (2 078)
Net profit/(loss) for the year |         3 347 |         2 656 |         2 910 |       (1 862)

Looking at the profitability of both companies, it appears as though Mr Price is more profitable than Foschini.
(a) State ONE area of profitability in which Foschini fared better than Mr Price, and give TWO reasons for your answer.
(b) State the MAIN reason why Mr Price is more profitable than Foschini.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Area where Foschini fared better (1 mark) + two reasons (2 marks) ✓✓✓:
• Sales / gross profit: Foschini's sales grew more than the previous year; Foschini's mark-up improved year on year while Mr Price's did not; Foschini's mark-up is higher (94,1% vs 68,7%). (Any reasonable point based on sales / gross profit / mark-up.)

(b) Main reason Mr Price is more profitable (1 mark) ✓: Mr Price has much better control over its operating expenses (operating expenses on sales 26,6% vs Foschini's 43,8%).

Teaching point: A high mark-up alone does not make a company more profitable — Foschini has the bigger margin but its operating expenses swallow it, so Mr Price's tighter cost control wins on the bottom line.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Comparing profitability

subQuestions.questionText:
Financial indicators — Net profit on sales: Mr Price 2022 12,5%, 2021 12,3%; Foschini 2022 6,7%, 2021 −5,7%. Net profit for the year (R'm): Mr Price 2022 3 347, 2021 2 656; Foschini 2022 2 910, 2021 −1 862.

(a) Describe what the financial indicator 'net profit on sales' shows.
(b) Who do you think would be most pleased with their 2022 net profit — the directors of Mr Price or the directors of Foschini? Explain your reasoning.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) ✓✓: It shows the percentage of sales left as net profit after subtracting all expenses — the possible amount available to shareholders (from which dividends could be paid).

(b) ✓✓✓: The directors of FOSCHINI would be most pleased.
• Although Mr Price's net profit is higher in rand terms, its net profit on sales only improved by 0,2% (12,3% → 12,5%), whereas Foschini's improved by 12,4% (−5,7% → 6,7%) — an excellent turnaround.
• Mr Price's net profit rose by R691m (26%), but Foschini's rose by R4 772m (256,28%), from a loss to a solid profit.

Teaching point: 'Most pleased' is about the improvement and recovery, not just the absolute figure — Foschini swung from a large loss to a healthy profit.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Net profit on sales

subQuestions.questionText:
Consolidated Statements of Financial Position (R'm) on 31 March 2022 — current assets:
                              | Mr Price 2022 | Foschini 2022
Inventories                    |         3 956 |         9 349
Trade and other receivables    |         2 749 |         8 975
Cash and cash equivalents      |         4 676 |         5 746
Current assets                 |        11 381 |        24 070

Mr Price's advantage over competitors is that 84% of its sales are cash sales. Explain, by studying the current assets only, how this has affected its liquidity compared with Foschini. Quote calculations in your explanation.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓✓✓:
• Mr Price's Trade and Other Receivables are only 24,15% of its total current assets (2 749 ÷ 11 381), whereas for Foschini they are 37,29% (8 975 ÷ 24 070) — Mr Price has far less cash tied up in debtors.
• Cash and cash equivalents make up 41,09% of Mr Price's current assets (4 676 ÷ 11 381) but only 23,87% of Foschini's (5 746 ÷ 24 070) — Mr Price holds proportionally much more actual cash.

Teaching point: Because most of Mr Price's sales are for cash, its current assets are weighted towards cash rather than debtors, giving it stronger, more immediately available liquidity.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Effect of cash sales on liquidity

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Price: Sales 2022 R26 685m; Trade and other receivables 2022 R2 749m, 2021 R2 316m. Note: about 16% of Mr Price's sales are credit sales. Debtors' collection period for 2021 was 244 days.

(a) Calculate the debtors' collection period for Mr Price for 2022.
(b) Explain why you think Mr Price has been / has not been cautious when granting credit.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Debtors' collection period (Mr Price 2022):
= [(2 749 + 2 316) ÷ 2] ÷ (26 685 × 16%) × 365
= 2 532,5 ÷ 4 269,6 × 365
= 216,5 days ✓✓✓

(b) ✓✓: Mr Price's debtors are taking 216,5 days (more than seven months) to pay. If Mr Price were being careful in selecting its credit customers, its debtors should be paying much faster — so on this evidence it has NOT been cautious enough.

Teaching point: Debtors' collection period = average debtors ÷ credit sales × 365; a period of over seven months signals weak credit vetting or collection.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Debtors' collection period

subQuestions.questionText:
Foschini: Cost of sales 2022 R22 343m; Inventories 2022 R9 349m, 2021 R8 336m. Stock turnover rate 2021 was 2,16 times. Foschini's director's report says 'inventory remains at levels which are sensible'.

(a) Calculate Foschini's stock turnover rate for 2022.
(b) Discuss, by providing reasons, whether or not you agree that Foschini's inventory is at a sensible level.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) Stock turnover rate (Foschini 2022):
= 22 343 ÷ [(9 349 + 8 336) ÷ 2]
= 22 343 ÷ 8 842,5
= 2,53 times ✓✓✓

(b) ✓✓: Disagree (or agree with reservations). Foschini only turns its stock about 2,5 times a year — it gets new stock roughly twice a year, which is not much for clothing and fashion products. Holding stock that long increases the risk of theft and of having to sell it on markdown / sales.

Teaching point: Stock turnover rate = cost of sales ÷ average inventory. For fashion retail, a low turnover (long holding period) risks obsolescence, markdowns and shrinkage.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Stock turnover rate

subQuestions.questionText:
Mr Price: Equity 2021 R10 838m; Shares in issue 2021 257 857 140.

Calculate the Net Asset Value per share for Mr Price for 2021.
subQuestions.memoText:
Net Asset Value per share (Mr Price 2021):
= 10 838 000 000 ÷ 257 857 140
= 4 203 cents = R42,03 per share ✓✓

Teaching point: NAV per share = ordinary shareholders' equity ÷ number of shares in issue — the book value backing each share.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Net Asset Value per share

subQuestions.questionText: Mr Price: Net asset value 2022 4 686 cents; closing share price on the JSE on 31 March 2022 21 651 cents. Why would an investor also consider the net asset value when studying the market value of Mr Price's shares?
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓:
• The NAV indicates whether the shares are overvalued or undervalued, which affects investor confidence in the company.
• It is the book value of the shares, so an investor can see by how much more (or less) the shares are trading on the JSE compared with their underlying net worth.

Teaching point: Comparing market price with NAV shows the premium (or discount) the market is placing on the company's future prospects.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - NAV versus market price

subQuestions.questionText:
Foschini: Dividends per share 2021 0 cents; Net profit/(loss) for the year 2021 −R1 862m; EPS 2021 −576 cents. Foschini's liquidity and solvency in 2021 were sound.

Foschini did not issue any dividends in 2021. Discuss whether or not this was a good decision.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓ (either view, with a valid reason):
Good decision:
• Foschini made a loss of R1 862m (−5,7% EPS). Paying dividends would have made the equity / retained income position worse. (Their liquidity and solvency were fine, so that would not be the reason.)
OR Not a good decision (1 mark only for a bare 'no'):
• Investors would have wanted dividends and may sell their shares because they received none.

Teaching point: Withholding dividends in a loss year protects equity and cash, though it can disappoint income-focused shareholders.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Dividend decision in a loss year

subQuestions.questionText:
Foschini 2022 (R'm): Total assets R43 313; Non-current liabilities R11 427; Current liabilities R12 748.

Calculate Foschini's solvency ratio for 2022 and then comment on it.
subQuestions.memoText:
Solvency ratio (Foschini 2022):
= 43 313 : (11 427 + 12 748)
= 43 313 : 24 175 ✓✓
= 1,79 : 1 ✓

Comment ✓: The assets are nearly twice the total liabilities, so Foschini is not at risk of going insolvent.

Teaching point: Solvency ratio = total assets : total liabilities; comfortably above 1 : 1 means the company owns enough to cover everything it owes.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Solvency ratio

subQuestions.questionText:
Foschini wants to carry on buying manufacturing plants in South Africa. Financial indicators for Foschini: Debt-equity ratio 2022 0,6 : 1, 2021 0,6 : 1; Return on capital employed 2022 9,5%, 2021 −6,8%; Average interest rate 2022 9,5%, 2021 8%.

By providing an in-depth analysis of the risk, gearing and return of The Foschini Group, would you, as a bank representative, lend them the money?
subQuestions.memoText:
In-depth analysis + conclusion ✓✓✓✓✓✓:
• Risk/gearing: the debt-equity ratio is 0,6 : 1 — still fairly low to medium risk.
• Gearing effect: Foschini's return on capital employed is 9,5% and the average interest rate is also 9,5%, so they are neither positively nor negatively geared (borrowing neither adds to nor subtracts from shareholder returns).
• Return trend: return on capital employed has recovered strongly, from −6,8% to 9,5% — an improvement of 16,3 percentage points, and hopefully they will keep increasing profit and return.
• Conclusion (any that makes sense): I would take the chance and lend them the money — risk is moderate and the trend is strongly positive.

Teaching point: A lending decision weighs the gearing level (debt-equity), whether the company earns more on capital than it pays in interest (positive gearing), and the direction of the return trend.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Lending decision (risk, gearing, return)

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 2.6.1. The other financing option is to issue more shares.
(a) Write down ONE advantage of issuing more shares over expanding the loan.
(b) It is said that issuing shares is a more expensive way of financing than taking out a loan. Discuss, by providing TWO reasons, why some people think this.
subQuestions.memoText:
(a) ✓: The debt-equity ratio will be positively affected (improve); OR they save on interest.

(b) ✓✓: Investors expect dividends on a regular basis, and the dividends could be more than the interest. When a loan is paid off the interest stops, whereas the shares stay in issue permanently and dividends are expected to increase every year.

Teaching point: A loan is a temporary, fixed cost that ends when repaid; shares are permanent and carry an open-ended, growing dividend expectation — which can make equity the dearer long-run option.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Shares versus loan financing

subQuestions.questionText: The director's report states that Foschini continues to suffer from crime-related incidents in South Africa. Discuss the role that the internal auditor has in preventing crime from within the business.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓: The internal auditors analyse where the problem areas or weak points are (in processes and controls) and then put controls in place to fix them, reducing the opportunity for internal crime.

Teaching point: Internal audit prevents internal fraud by identifying control weaknesses and strengthening the procedures around them, not by investigating after the fact.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Role of the internal auditor

subQuestions.questionText:
198 Foschini stores were damaged in the July 2021 civil unrest. The Group performed an assessment to identify whether the losses related to store assets should be capitalised or treated as repairs and maintenance.

Explain how they would decide whether the cost of repairs to the stores would be added to Land and Buildings (capitalised) or treated as Repairs and Maintenance.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓:
• If the repair INCREASES the value of the store (an improvement beyond its original condition), the cost should be capitalised (added to Land and Buildings).
• If the repair merely restores the store to the value / condition it was in before it was damaged, it should be treated as Repairs and Maintenance (an expense).

Teaching point: Capitalise spending that enhances an asset beyond its original state; expense spending that only maintains or restores its existing condition.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Capitalise versus expense

subQuestions.questionText:
RECONCILIATIONS — LAVENDER COTTAGE (sells home accessories; owned by Liyah Pillay).

Statement received from the creditor Kitchenware Suppliers, dated 30 November 2023 (statement no. 73):
Aug 1 Balance R54 240 | Aug 12 Invoice 63 R42 480 (Dr), balance R96 720 | Sept 20 EFT R30 000 (Cr), balance R66 720 | Sept 20 Discount R1 500 (Cr), balance R65 220 | Sept 27 Invoice 82 R49 700 (Dr), balance R114 920 | Oct 1 Interest R379 (Dr), balance R115 299 | Oct 2 Credit note 37 R12 500 (Cr), balance R102 799 | Oct 31 Invoice 91 R63 200 (Dr), balance R165 999 | Nov 1 Interest R1 412 (Dr), balance R167 411 | Nov 20 EFT R47 411 (Cr), balance R120 000.
Terms & conditions: 5% discount granted if paid within 30 days of statement date; 20% p.a. interest charged monthly on amounts 60 days overdue; credit limit of R120 000.

Study the statement. Kitchenware Suppliers has three terms and conditions. Analyse whether Kitchenware Suppliers enforced these, and whether Lavender Cottage adhered to them.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓✓:
• Discount: Kitchenware Suppliers granted a discount (20 Sept) when there was still an amount owing from more than 30 days back — they did NOT stick to their own term.
• Interest: they charged interest only after 60 days overdue — they DID stick to this term.
• Credit limit: they did NOT enforce the R120 000 credit limit — the balance was allowed to run above it (R165 999) before the November EFT brought it back down.

Teaching point: Checking a supplier statement against its stated terms shows whether the supplier applied its own rules and whether the customer stayed within them.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Evaluating terms and conditions

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 3.1. Fill in the age analysis as it would appear at the bottom of the statement from Kitchenware Suppliers. Ignore all errors and omissions and use ONLY the figures given in the statement. Show all the figures that go into each block (you do not need to total each block). Columns: 90 Days | 60 Days | 30 Days | Current.
subQuestions.memoText:
AGE ANALYSIS (statement figures only):
90 Days: 54 240 + 42 480 (= 96 720) − 31 500 − 47 411 (November EFT and September payment applied to the oldest balance) ✓
60 Days: 49 700 − 12 500 (Invoice 82 less Credit note 37) ✓
30 Days: 379 + 63 200 (Interest + Invoice 91) ✓
Current: 1 412 (November interest) ✓

1 mark for correctly identifying the invoices over 90, 60 and 30 days: 96 720, 49 700, 63 200.

Teaching point: An age analysis buckets the balance by how long each item has been outstanding; payments are applied to the oldest amounts first.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Age analysis

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 3.1. If you worked for Lavender Cottage and were in charge of paying the creditors, explain ONE change you would make to how Lavender Cottage pays their creditors (based on how they pay Kitchenware Suppliers). Explain why you would make this change.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓ (suggestion) + ✓ (reason):
• Any suggestion that ensures Lavender Cottage pays more regularly / on time to help cash flow, OR that prevents them breaking the credit terms and getting a bad reputation and being charged more interest.
  e.g. 'Pay each supplier in full within 30 days of the statement date' — reason: 'to earn the 5% settlement discount and avoid the 20% p.a. interest and damage to the relationship.'

Teaching point: Paying within the discount period saves the discount, avoids interest penalties, and protects the supplier relationship and future credit terms.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Improving creditor payment practice

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 3.1. Errors and omissions found when comparing the statement with Kitchenware Suppliers' account in Lavender Cottage's creditors' ledger:
1. Lavender Cottage incorrectly recorded Invoice 63 as R44 280 (should be R42 480).
2. The discount on 20 September should not have been granted by Kitchenware Suppliers; Lavender Cottage did not record it in their creditors' ledger.
3. Credit note 37 was actually for R15 200; Lavender Cottage correctly recorded R15 200 in their creditors' ledger.
4. The interest on 1 November was incorrectly calculated by Kitchenware Suppliers; no interest for 1 November had been entered in Lavender Cottage's creditors' ledger; the interest should have been R1 087.

Statement balance (incorrect): R120 000. Creditors' ledger balance (incorrect): R119 188.

Reconcile the statement to the ledger: show the amounts that go into the Creditor's Reconciliation Statement and the amounts that would be entered into the creditors' ledger account.
subQuestions.memoText:
CREDITOR'S RECONCILIATION (Do not calculate the totals):

                       | Reconciliation Statement | Creditors' Ledger
Incorrect balance      | 120 000                  | 119 188
1. Invoice 63          |                          | (1 800) ✓  (44 280 − 42 480 overstated in the ledger)
2. Discount            | 1 500 ✓                  |            (add back — the discount should not have been granted, so the statement is understated)
3. Credit note 37      | (2 700) ✓                |            (statement shows R12 500 instead of R15 200; reduce the statement by R2 700)
4. Interest            | 1 087 − 1 412 = (325) ✓  | 1 087 ✓  (statement interest overstated by R325; the R1 087 must still be entered in the ledger)
Corrected balance      | DO NOT CALCULATE         | DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: The supplier's errors (wrong discount, wrong credit note, wrong interest) are corrected on the Reconciliation Statement side; the business's own errors and omissions (invoice recorded at the wrong amount, interest not entered) are corrected in the Creditors' Ledger account.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Reconciliation statement and ledger

subQuestions.questionText:
Liyah sends employees to the shops with the business credit card to buy packing material, refreshments and small items of trading stock. A whistle-blower told her that some of these employees are buying things for themselves with Lavender Cottage's credit card.

Discuss a control system that the internal auditors could put in place to stop employees from buying personal items with the business' credit card.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marked with a rubric — 3 marks for a cheap, easy control that should genuinely stop the abuse ✓✓✓. Example of a full-mark answer:
• Only ONE employee is authorised to use the business credit card.
• That employee must carry a list of items to buy, signed by Liyah or a manager.
• On return, Liyah or someone in finance compares the till slip against the approved list.

Teaching point: An effective control over a shared payment instrument restricts who may use it, pre-authorises what may be bought, and reconciles the receipts against the authorisation afterwards.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Internal control over a business credit card
